summary: A scholar in sinology and history/archaeology, Étienne Balazs studied under Otto Franke from 1923 to 1930. He held posts at the Centre national de la recherche scientifique in 1949 and at the University of Paris from around 1955 to 1963.

Étienne Lamotte worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, studying at KU Leuven, Sapienza University of Rome, and the University of Paris under Louis de La Vallée Poussin and others. He held long-term posts at Catholic University of Louvain and KU Leuven.

A scholar of Iranian/Central Asian studies, linguistics, and history/archaeology, Étienne Marc Quatremère studied under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He was a professor at Faculté des Lettres de Rouen, Collège de France (1819–1857), and Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales (1827–1857).

A scholar in Buddhist studies, Ñāṇamoli Thera studied at Exeter College, Oxford, around 1923 to 1926. He also studied under traditional teachers Nyanatiloka Mahathera in 1949 and Palane Vajiranana in 1950.

Active in Indology and philosophy, Óscar Cortés studied at the University of Guadalajara (2007–2013) and El Colegio de México (2015–2017). He served as a researcher at Palabra de Clío from 2018 to 2020.

Ösel Tendzin, active in Buddhist studies, studied at Fordham University and under traditional teachers Satchidananda Saraswati and Chögyam Trungpa. He served as executive vice president of Vajradhatu in 1973 and succeeded Trungpa in 1987.

Working in religious studies and Indology, Ülo Valk studied at the University of Tartu from around 1980 to 1986. He held a post at the University of Tartu around 1995 and served as an editor for Numen around 2006 to 2018.

A scholar of Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Indology, Čedomil Veljačić studied at the University of Zagreb and the University of Bonn. In 1961, he became a lecturer and assistant professor of Asian philosophy at the University of Zagreb.
Active in Indology and linguistics, Čeněk Vyhnis studied at Charles University from 1864 to 1867 under Alfred Ludwig. In 1891, he held a post at Charles University as gymnasium professor of classics.
